title:
Getting started on the
Illinois Campus Cluster
body: A practical workflow for data analysis
notes: Hi everyone, I’m from Kun Wang’s lab. We mainly do computational work, so for us, HPC is a bit like the lab bench in a wet lab—it’s where we run our analyses. Today, I’ll give you a brief introduction to the Illinois Campus Cluster and walk through the basic skills you need to run computationally intensive analyses on it.

title: Prepare files on login nodes; run jobs on compute nodes
notes:
Before we connect, it helps to know what we’re connecting to. HPC means high-performance computing. A cluster is a group of connected computers, and each computer is called a node. In this diagram, our laptop connects to the head node, which we’ll call the login node.

That’s where we organize files, edit scripts, and submit work. Other people share this node, so we use compute nodes for the heavier analysis. To do that, we submit a job: we tell the scheduler what program we want to run and what resources it needs. The scheduler starts it when those resources are available.

Both kinds of node can access the project files through shared storage. Connecting with VS Code gives us access to those files, but it doesn’t reserve a compute node. Before any of this works, we need an approved account and permission to use the group’s resources.

title: Request access and confirm your allocation details
body:
Existing lab accessAsk your PI or technical contact which cluster group to join.
A new computing needStart an Illinois Computes request.
Detail to confirmUsed for
NetIDYour login identity
Slurm accountThe group’s assigned computing resources
PartitionA queue you may submit to
Project pathA folder where you have permission to save files
Research access request ↗Illinois Computes request ↗

Before connecting: get account approval, confirm these four details, and set up Duo.
notes:
For access, I’d start with your PI or the person who manages computing for your group. If the group already uses the cluster, they can tell you which group to join. You may see the term investor group—that means a lab or organization that has arranged cluster resources. For a new computing need, Illinois Computes is another starting point. The form starts the request; we still need approval and account setup before we can log in.

There are four details we’ll use throughout the talk. Your NetID identifies you. Your Slurm account identifies the group resources your job can use, so it isn’t the same as your NetID. Slurm is the software that schedules jobs. The partition is a queue of eligible resources, and the project path tells us where we can save files.

Ask for an account and partition that work together, a folder you can write to, and help setting up Duo if needed. Anywhere you see something like YOUR_NETID, replace it with your own value. With those details ready, we can try the first connection.

title: The first SSH login
body:
On your laptop: open Terminal (macOS) or PowerShell (Windows)
ssh YOUR_NETID@cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

ssh starts the connection · before @: your user name · after @: the cluster address

1 · Run the commandReplace YOUR_NETID, then press Enter.
2 · PasswordType your NetID password and press Enter; typing stays hidden.
3 · DuoFollow the prompt and approve the authentication request.
notes:
We’ll start with a quick connection from the laptop. On a Mac, open Terminal; on Windows, open PowerShell. If Windows doesn’t recognize ssh, you’ll need to enable the OpenSSH Client first.

In this line, ssh starts the connection. Your NetID goes before the at sign, and the cluster address goes after it. Replace YOUR_NETID, leave the hostname as shown, and press Enter.

The first time, SSH may ask you to confirm the server’s identity. Check that fingerprint against institutional guidance or with support before accepting it. If you get an unexpected warning that the host has changed, check that too. Then enter your NetID password. You won’t see anything appear as you type—that’s normal. Complete the Duo prompt on your registered device. ICC uses your password and Duo here, rather than user-created SSH keys.

Once we see the welcome message and a command prompt, we’re connected. The prompt tells us the shell is ready, and commands typed here run on the cluster. The screenshot is an older example, so its dates and quota numbers aren’t current guidance. We can type exit to close this test connection without deleting anything. VS Code will make its own connection, so let’s look at that tool next.

title: VS Code is an editor for code and project files
body:
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft’s code editor for working with scripts and project files.

B · ExplorerBrowse files and folders in the left sidebar.
C · EditorRead and edit scripts in the main area.
D · TerminalEnter commands in the bottom panel.
notes:
This is Visual Studio Code, or just VS Code. It’s Microsoft’s editor for code and project files. The useful thing is that we can browse files, edit them, and use a terminal in one window. When I say script, I mean a text file containing instructions for a program to run.

This screenshot is Microsoft’s example, so we won’t be using these particular files or this code. The area marked B is Explorer, where we browse folders and files. The areas marked C show the files we’ve opened in the editor. Down at D is the terminal, where we enter commands. That bottom panel can show other things too, but here it’s showing a terminal.

Those are the three areas we’ll keep coming back to: files on the left, editing in the main area, and commands in the terminal. We can also use this same window to work with files on the cluster.

title: Files stay on the cluster; terminal commands run there
body:
LOCAL Your laptop
VS Code window
View and editanalysis.pyYour screen, keyboard, and mouse
Remote - SSH
⟷
View · edit · save
REMOTE The cluster
Project filesdemo/analysis.pySave updates this file.
Remote terminalCommands run on the cluster.

In the SSH window, saves update cluster files and terminal commands run on the connected host.
notes:
Here’s why I recommend VS Code for this workflow. The window stays on our laptop, and the Remote - SSH extension connects it to the cluster. Suppose we’ve opened analysis.py in that connected window. We’re looking at it on the laptop, but the file itself is demo/analysis.py on the cluster. When we press Save, that remote file is the one that changes. We don’t need to download a copy, edit it, and upload it again each time. This picture shows where we’ll end up after uploading the project; we’ll walk through those steps in a moment.

The terminal works in a similar way. We see it on the laptop screen, but its commands run on the connected cluster host. Our first connection goes to a login node. If we opened a separate local terminal, its commands would run on the laptop instead. Later, an interactive job will let us open a shell on a compute node, so we’ll check which host we’re using.

We’ll still use Slurm to get resources for an analysis; connecting the editor doesn’t reserve a compute node. For everyday file work, we can open, edit, and save directly in this window. To get that working, we need VS Code and the Remote - SSH extension on the laptop.

title: Install VS Code and the Remote - SSH extension
body:
First: download and open VS Code on your laptop.

The editor and Remote - SSH extension are installed on your laptop.
notes:
There are two things to install on the laptop. First, download VS Code for your operating system, install it, and open it. Then click the Extensions icon in the sidebar. Extensions are add-ons that give the editor extra features.

Search for Remote - SSH and look for Microsoft as the publisher. The screenshot is an older official UI example, but the part to look for is the same: Microsoft as the publisher and the Install button. Install the current version and wait for it to finish. That adds the commands we need to connect to the cluster.

At this point, we’ve prepared the editor on the laptop. We’ll set up Python and the analysis packages on the cluster separately, when we get to software setup.

To start the connection, we’ll use something called the Command Palette. It’s a searchable menu of VS Code actions, so we can type the name of the action we want. We’ll use it with the same NetID and cluster hostname that worked in our SSH test.

title: Connecting VS Code with Remote - SSH
body:
1
Choose Connect to Host…Cmd+Shift+P (Mac) · Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows/Linux)
Search: Remote-SSH: Connect to Host
2
Enter your login address
Use this address:YOUR_NETID@
cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

Password + Duo
Choose Linux if asked.

notes:
To open the Command Palette, press Command-Shift-P on a Mac, or Control-Shift-P on Windows or Linux. Search for Remote-SSH: Connect to Host. Then enter your NetID and the cluster hostname, just as we did in the terminal connection.

You’ll go through the password and Duo prompts again. If VS Code asks which operating system the remote computer uses, choose Linux—that’s what the cluster runs. It may open a separate connected window.

To check that it worked, look at the SSH indicator in the lower-left corner. It should name the cluster host. That tells us this window is connected to the remote computer. If it seems stuck waiting, check the Remote - SSH output or login terminal; there may be an authentication prompt waiting for a response.

Once we’re connected, we need somewhere to put our project. We’ll choose that location before uploading the files.

title: Choose home, project, or scratch storage
body:
LocationUse it forLimits and actions
/u/YOUR_NETIDSettings and small personal filesVery limited quota: 100 GiB (soft limit). Keep large datasets elsewhere.
/projects/YOUR_GROUPGroup data, software, and retained outputsShared group quota. Keep backups: no snapshots are kept for file recovery.
/scratch/YOUR_NETIDTemporary working dataTemporary only: files typically deleted after 30 days without access, sometimes sooner.

Use your group’s full project path; /projects/YOUR_GROUP is a placeholder.
notes:
Before we upload anything, we need to choose where it will live. Home, project, and scratch storage have different jobs.

Home, under /u, is for settings and small personal files. It has a very limited quota, which means a limit on how much space you can use: 100 GiB as the documented soft limit and 103 GiB as the hard limit. If you stay above the soft limit for seven days, new writes stop until you reduce your usage. You can’t expand the home quota, so it’s a poor place to collect large datasets.

Project storage is shared by the group, and the available space depends on its allocation. It has no snapshots—saved filesystem states that let you recover earlier files—so important data need a separate backup plan.

Scratch is temporary workspace. Files are typically deleted after 30 days without access, sometimes sooner if space is tight. Once purged, they can’t be recovered, so move valuable outputs elsewhere.

For our project, we’ll use the full path supplied by the group, where we have permission to save files. The path on the slide is a placeholder. We’ll open that parent folder first, then upload demo into it.

body:

/projects/YOUR_GROUP

Explorer now shows the remote destination.

We’ve chosen a storage location, so we can open it in VS Code. In the connected window, go to File, then Open Folder, and enter your approved group path. Here, /projects/YOUR_GROUP stands for the parent folder where we’ll put demo.

Microsoft’s screenshot uses a path from its own example system. Yours should be the full path your group gave you. Also check that the SSH indicator still names the cluster. With that connection active, the folders in Explorer are on the remote computer.

At this point, we’ve opened the destination, but we haven’t uploaded anything yet. The demo folder is still on the laptop. It helps to keep those two locations clear: the folder we’re taking from the laptop, and the folder we’re putting it into on the cluster. Next, we’ll make that transfer.

Once the transfer finishes, use File, Open Folder again and open the uploaded demo folder. The example path is /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo; yours will use the group’s actual location. Expand data and open samples.csv. We should see a header and three sample rows. That checks that the file arrived and we can read it on the cluster.

From here, Command-S or Control-S saves our edits directly to the remote file. Dragging files is convenient for this small example. For a large dataset, use the transfer service your group recommends, such as Globus, and check that the transfer finishes before starting the analysis.

Our files are in place. We can open a terminal in this same project folder next.

title: Open a terminal in the same project
body:
1
Terminal → New TerminalIn your remote VS Code window
hostnameWhich computer?
Expect a login node.
cd /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demoMove into your uploaded project.
Use your group’s actual path.
pwdWhich folder?
Check the full project path.

Run one line, press Enter, wait for the prompt, then continue.
notes:
We’ve been working with files through the interface. For the next steps, we’ll also use a few commands. In the remote VS Code window, choose Terminal, then New Terminal. The terminal is the text window; the shell is the program that reads what we type. Here, that shell runs on the connected cluster host. The screenshot is Microsoft’s example of a remote terminal. Their uname command reports Linux; our three checks below will confirm the host and folder in our own session.

We’ll use these three lines one at a time. hostname tells us which computer we’re on. At this stage, we expect a login host, such as cc-login1. Then cd changes the current folder to our uploaded project. Use your group’s full path in place of the example. Finally, pwd prints the full path, so we can check that the terminal is working in the same folder we opened in Explorer. If cd works, it usually doesn’t print anything.

When the prompt comes back, the shell is ready for another command. In our examples, the dollar sign marks that prompt; we don’t type it ourselves. These short file checks are fine on the login node. We’ll send the actual analysis to compute resources later. First, we’ll break down how a command is written.

title: Read the program, options, and path in a command
body:
head -n 5 data/samples.csv
Programhead displays the beginning of a text file.
Option + value-n 5 asks for the first five lines.
File pathdata/samples.csv is the path to the file to read.

Quotes keep a path together: head -n 5 "data/samples.csv". They are required for paths containing spaces.
notes:
A command can look like a long string at first, but we can read this one in three parts. head is the program we’re asking to run. The option -n, followed by 5, says we want the first five lines. Then data/samples.csv tells it which file to read. If the file has fewer than five lines, it just shows the lines that are there.

Everything after head is an argument. Some arguments change what the program does; others give it a value or a filename. An option letter belongs to that particular command, so the same letter can mean something else in a different program.

Spaces usually separate the arguments. If a path contains spaces, quotes keep the whole path together. The quoted example on this slide works too, but this particular path doesn’t need quotes because it has no spaces.

We’ll use this way of reading commands throughout the talk. Before trying more file commands, we need to know how the folder we’re currently in affects the path we type.

title: Use pwd and cd to move through the project
body:
Type commands after $; other lines are output
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ cd data
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo/data
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
pwdPrint the current folder.
cd dataEnter the data subfolder.
cd ..Go up to the parent folder.

. = current folder · .. = parent folder

/projects/… starts at the filesystem root; data/… starts from the current folder.
notes:
Once we’re in the terminal, the first thing I want to know is where we are. That’s what pwd tells us. Here, we’re starting in demo. We type what comes after the dollar sign; the other lines are the computer’s response.

cd data takes us into the data folder. It usually prints nothing, so the next pwd lets us see the new location. cd .. takes us one level up, back to demo, and pwd confirms it again. Two dots mean the parent folder; one dot means the current folder.

A path beginning with a slash is an absolute path: it gives the location from the filesystem root. A relative path, like data, starts wherever we are now. Capitalization matters in file and folder names.

That covers moving into a folder and going up one level. Next, let’s look at two shortcuts for moving home and coming back.

title: Use cd ~ for home and cd - to go back
body:
Continue from demo on the previous page
$ cd ~
$ pwd
/u/YOUR_NETID
$ cd -
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
cd ~Go to your home folder.
cd -Return to the previous folder and print its path.
pwdConfirm where the terminal is now.

cd .. means parent folder. cd - means previous folder.
notes:
We’re still in demo. cd ~ takes us to our home folder, shown here as /u/YOUR_NETID. The tilde is a shortcut for home. We run pwd to confirm that move.

Now cd - takes us back to the folder we were in before, so here we return to demo. It also prints the destination itself. That’s why the same path appears again when we run pwd.

It helps to keep these two ideas separate. cd .. goes to a parent folder in the directory tree. cd - goes to the previous location, even if it’s somewhere else in that tree.

We’re back in demo now. Let’s list what’s inside data without moving into it.

title: List visible and hidden names with ls
body:
Illustrative data folder; commands run from demo
$ ls data
counts.tsv  samples.csv
$ ls -a data
.  ..  counts.tsv  samples.csv
ls dataList visible file and folder names inside data.
ls -a dataInclude hidden names beginning with a dot.

. is this folder; .. is its parent. Later, ls -a in demo will also show .venv.

counts.tsv is a larger illustrative file. The supplied demo uses samples.csv.
notes:
We’ve found the folder. To see what’s inside, we use ls. Both commands here list data, and our terminal stays in demo throughout. For this illustration, imagine there’s also a larger file called counts.tsv. The supplied demo still uses the small samples.csv.

Plain ls shows the visible names. Add -a, and it also shows names beginning with a dot. That includes the single dot for this folder and the two dots for its parent. Later, we’ll run ls -a in demo to see .venv, the hidden folder holding our Python environment.

These commands show us which names exist. On the next page, we’ll add file details and make the sizes easier to read.

title: Show file details and readable sizes with ls
body:
-l: details · -h: readable sizes · -a: include hidden names

Illustrative listing; total lines omitted
$ ls -l data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 25165824 Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group       58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lh data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group  24M Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group   58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lah data
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 3 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group  24M Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group   58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv

Same file: 25165824 bytes → 24M (24 MiB). Folder size here is not the total of its contents.
notes:
Now we’re asking ls to show more detail. With -l, each line gives permissions, a link count, the owner and group, the size, the modification time, and the name. The filename and size are usually the first things I check. The users and dates here are examples.

The larger file makes -h easier to see. With -l, counts.tsv shows 25165824 bytes. Add -h and that becomes 24M, meaning 24 MiB in these 1024-based units. Nothing happened to the file; we’ve just changed how the size is displayed. The small samples.csv is still 58 bytes, so its number stays the same.

We can combine the letters as -lah to get details, readable sizes, and hidden entries together. A folder’s size on this line isn’t the total of everything inside it. We’ll use du for that.

Now that we can inspect what’s there, let’s look at making folders and copying files.

title: Create folders with mkdir and copy files with cp
body:
CommandResult
mkdir resultsCreate one new folder.
mkdir -p results/qcCreate missing folders along the path; accept existing folders.
cp -i notes.txt notes_backup.txtCopy a file; ask before overwriting.
cp -r data data_backupCopy the folder and its subfolders to a new destination.

cp: source first, destination second. The source stays in place.

Check the result with ls. Copying a large dataset also uses extra storage.
notes:
These are common operations for organizing a project. We can do most of them in VS Code’s Explorer too, but it’s useful to recognize the commands in instructions. These are examples to choose from, rather than a required setup sequence.

mkdir results makes a new folder. If it’s already there, plain mkdir reports an error. In mkdir -p results/qc, -p creates missing folders along the path and accepts folders that already exist.

For cp, the source comes first and the destination second. cp -i notes.txt notes_backup.txt makes a copy and asks before replacing an existing destination file. The original stays in place. With cp -r, we copy the folder and its subfolders. Here, data_backup is a new destination. A large dataset will also take more storage when we copy it.

These commands often finish quietly. Use ls to check what changed. Next, we’ll look at moving a file and deleting an unwanted copy.

title: Move or rename with mv; remove a file with rm
body:
Move or rename: source first, destination second
mv -i notes_backup.txt notes_old.txt

Rename the backup; -i asks before replacing an existing destination file.

Remove the unwanted copy
rm -i notes_old.txt

-i asks before deleting. Check the filename before confirming.

Shell deletion normally has no Trash recovery. Check the result with ls.
notes:
Suppose we made notes_backup.txt and want to give it a different name. mv -i notes_backup.txt notes_old.txt renames it. The source comes first and the destination second, just as with cp. If the destination were a different folder, mv would move the file there. The -i asks before replacing an existing destination.

If we no longer need that copy, rm -i notes_old.txt asks before deleting it. Check the filename before confirming, because shell deletion normally has no Trash recovery.

After either operation, ls lets us check the result. We’ve covered organizing files; next, we’ll read a small input file without changing it.

title: Inspecting a small text file
body:
CommandUse
cat notes.txtPrint the entire small file
head -n 5 data/samples.csvPrint up to 5 lines from the start
less notes.txtBrowse text; press q to leave
Output of head for the included sample table
sample_id,reads
sample_A,1000
sample_B,1500
sample_C,1200

Preview a few rows before running the analysis. Avoid printing a huge file with cat.
notes:
Sometimes we just need a quick look at a file. cat prints the whole text file in the terminal, which works well for a short note or a small configuration file. For something large, I’d start with head so the terminal doesn’t fill up with thousands of lines.

We’ve already seen how to read head -n 5. Here is its output for samples.csv: the file has only four lines, so it shows all four. The first gives us the column names, and the other three contain our sample names and example values. The commas separate the fields.

For a longer text file, less gives us a viewer we can scroll through. Press q when we’re done, and we’re back at the shell prompt. These tools read ordinary text. Images, saved R objects, and other binary files need a suitable viewer. We can also open small text files directly in VS Code.

Once we can read a file, the next useful step is finding a particular file or a line inside it.

title: Find a file, then find text inside it
body:
Search filenames within data and its subfolders
find data -type f -name "*.csv"
-type f / -nameKeep files only / match their names against the pattern.
"*.csv"The * matches any text before .csv.
Search inside this file; -n includes line numbers
grep -n "sample_B" data/samples.csv
Expected grep output: line 3 contains the match
3:sample_B,1500
notes:
There are two kinds of searching here. We might know the kind of file we want, or we might know some text that should be inside it.

find handles the first case. Here, data tells it where to start searching, and -type f keeps regular files in the results. Then -name checks their names against the pattern. In "*.csv", the star can stand for any text before .csv. The quotes let find receive that pattern directly, without the shell expanding it first. In our small project, it should return data/samples.csv.

grep searches the text inside a file. Here, we’re looking for sample_B in samples.csv. The -n adds a line number, so 3:sample_B,1500 tells us the match is on line three.

Both commands leave the file unchanged. Starting in the relevant project folder helps keep the results manageable. We’ve found our file and a specific row; next, we can check how many lines it contains and how much storage it uses.

title: Count lines and check disk usage
body:
Run this command
wc -l data/samples.csv
Expected output; do not type this line
4 data/samples.csv
wc -lCount lines in this text file.
4 linesOne header plus three sample rows.
Check space used by the input folder
du -sh data

-s gives one summary total · -h uses readable units such as K or M

wc -l includes header lines. du shows space used; quota shows usage and limits.
notes:
A quick line count can help us check an input file before we run anything. Here, wc -l returns four, followed by the filename. That’s one header line and three sample rows. Strictly speaking, it counts newline characters; all four lines in this example end with one.

We do need to know the file format before treating that number as a sample count. A different file might have comments, several header lines, or one record spread over multiple lines.

For storage, du -sh data tells us how much disk space the data folder uses. The -s asks for one summary total, and -h gives us readable units like K or M. The exact value can vary with the filesystem.

That tells us what the folder is using. To see how much storage we’re allowed to use as well, we run quota, which reports usage and limits for the filesystem areas we can access. We don’t have to memorize all these options; the next slide shows where to look them up.

title: Help and everyday terminal shortcuts
body:
Command / keyWhat it does
man lsOpen the manual; press q to leave
head --helpShow the Linux command’s built-in help
TabComplete a file or folder name
↑ / historyRecall previous commands / list shell history
Ctrl+CInterrupt the command currently running in this terminal
clear / exitClear the display / leave the current shell

Keep this login shell open for job submission; exit closes it.
notes:
You don’t need to learn every command option by heart. I’d much rather know how to look one up. man ls opens the manual for ls, and q gets us out of that viewer. Many programs also have --help, like head does here. These examples are for the cluster’s Linux shell; the tools on a laptop can have slightly different options.

A few keyboard shortcuts make everyday work easier. Tab completes file and folder names. The up arrow brings back a previous command, so we can check it or edit it before pressing Enter. history shows a list of earlier commands.

Ctrl+C interrupts the command currently using this terminal. A batch job submitted separately through Slurm keeps running. clear just clears the display. exit leaves the current shell, so what it closes depends on where we are: it could leave a compute allocation or end the SSH connection.

For now, we’ll keep this login shell open. We have the file commands we need, so we can move on to submitting a job.

title: Slurm runs work on allocated resources
body:
LOGIN NODE
Prepare and submithello.sbatchYour terminal stays here.
sbatch→
SlurmWait for resourcesThe scheduler
Allocate→
COMPUTE NODE
Run the jobhello.sbatchThe program runs here.
↕↕
Same shared demo/ folderInput · scripts · output

Batch: submit a script. Interactive: request a compute shell with srun.

Submit on the login node; the job runs on an allocated compute node.
notes:
This is where Slurm comes in. We prepare the script on the login node, then use sbatch to send it to the scheduler. Slurm checks the resources we’ve requested and may put the job in a queue until they’re available. Once it allocates those resources, meaning reserves them for our job, the program runs on a compute node.

The shared folder underneath the diagram connects the two sides. Both nodes can access our approved project folder, so the job can read the inputs and write its outputs there. We don’t have to copy the whole project to another computer each time. Slurm is the scheduling software in the middle; the files stay in that shared storage.

Our terminal stays on the login node after submission. The batch job can keep running even if we disconnect the laptop. Later, we’ll also use an interactive job, which gives us a shell on allocated compute resources for software setup.

First, though, we’ll look inside hello.sbatch and see what we’re actually asking Slurm to do.

title: Read a Slurm batch script line by line
body:
Select a line

Use the Slurm account assigned to your group.

01Use Bash to read the commands.
02Give the job a recognizable name.
03Use the Slurm account assigned to your group.
04Use a partition that this account can access.
05Request one compute node.
06Request one task for this program.
07Reserve one CPU for that task.
08Request 1 GiB of RAM per node.
09Set a five-minute running-time limit.
10Print a message into the job output.

Edit these lines inside hello.sbatch in VS Code, then save. Submit it from the terminal after reviewing the resource settings.
notes:
This little file is the complete request for our first job. hello.sbatch is just plain text: it tells Slurm what resources we need, then tells the computer what to run.

The first line selects Bash to read the commands. The lines starting with #SBATCH are the settings for Slurm, and they go before the commands that run the program. The job name helps us recognize this submission. The account identifies our group’s compute allocation, and the partition selects a queue we can use. We need a valid account and partition pair from our group.

The next lines ask for nodes, tasks, CPUs per task, memory, and a running-time limit. At the bottom, echo prints the message. The five-minute limit starts when the job runs; time spent waiting in the queue doesn’t count.

We’ll edit and save this file in VS Code, then submit it with sbatch. If we ran bash hello.sbatch directly, Bash would treat the #SBATCH lines as comments and run the command on the current machine, without requesting resources.

Before submitting, I want to slow down on nodes, tasks, and CPUs, because those names are easy to mix up.

title: Set nodes, tasks, CPUs, memory, and time for a job
body:
Example resource request: count the node, the tasks, then the CPUs.

--nodes=11 computer
--ntasks=22 tasks in the whole job
--cpus-per-task=22 CPUs reserved for each task
Node 1One computer
Task 1One program process
CPUCPU
Task 2One program process
CPUCPU
2 tasks × 2 CPUs/task = 4 CPUs requestedntasks is already the total; do not multiply by nodes again.

Reserving resources does not launch the tasks or make the program parallel.

Keep hello.sbatch at: 1 node · 1 task · 1 CPU/task
--mem=1G1 GiB of RAM per node--time=00:05:00Runtime limit: hours:minutes:seconds
notes:
I find this easier to understand by counting the boxes. The big box is one node, so one computer. Inside it are two tasks, which represent two program processes across the whole job. Each task has two CPUs reserved. Two tasks times two CPUs per task gives us four CPUs in total. ntasks already counts tasks across all the nodes, so we don’t multiply by the node count again.

A task here isn’t a sample or a file. These boxes show what we’re requesting, rather than every CPU the computer physically has. Depending on the system, a Slurm CPU can mean a core or a hardware thread.

There’s another step between requesting resources and using them. Plain python analysis.py starts one process. Running multiple processes needs a suitable program and launcher, and a multithreaded program needs its own worker or thread setting.

For our actual hello job, we’ll keep it small: one node, one task, and one CPU. --mem=1G requests one GiB of RAM per node. That’s working memory, not disk storage. --time=00:05:00 allows five minutes of running time, with queue waiting excluded. For a real analysis, we’d choose these values based on the software and data.

With those settings clear, we’re ready to submit hello.sbatch.

title: Submit the first job: hello.sbatch
body:
In the remote demo folder, after saving the file
pwd
ls hello.sbatch
sbatch hello.sbatch
Example response; record the ID returned by your submission
Submitted batch job 123456

This first job prints a message. It does not run analysis.py yet.
notes:
We’ve checked the resource settings, so now save hello.sbatch in VS Code. In the remote demo folder, pwd confirms our location, and ls hello.sbatch checks that the saved file is there. Then sbatch hello.sbatch sends it to Slurm.

Slurm returns a job ID, shown here as 123456. Keep the number you actually receive. Accepted doesn’t mean started or finished: the job may still be waiting. This first job just prints a message; it doesn’t run analysis.py yet.

The submission happens in the terminal after saving the file. Pressing Run in the editor doesn’t submit a Slurm job. Next, we’ll use that returned job ID to check the queue and find the output.

title: Checking the queue and stopping a job
body:
-u selects your user; run squeue again to refresh
squeue -u YOUR_NETID
Illustration: job 123456
PD Pending Queued; check the reason
→
R Running Using allocated resources
→
No longer listed Read the output slurm-123456.out
Leaving the queue does not prove success.
Optional: cancel an unwanted job. Let hello finish here.
scancel 123456

After hello leaves the queue: cat slurm-123456.out → My first HPC job. Use your job ID.
notes:
We have a job ID. Now squeue -u YOUR_NETID lists your jobs, and -u selects the user. Each run gives a fresh snapshot.

Read the diagram from left to right. PD means pending; check the listed reason. R means running on allocated resources. This tiny job may finish before we check. Once it leaves the queue, read slurm-123456.out with cat, using your own job ID. We expect My first HPC job. Leaving the queue alone doesn’t prove success, so investigate missing or unexpected output.

scancel followed by the job ID is for a job we want to stop. We’ll let hello finish here. Ctrl+C in a separate log viewer doesn’t cancel a submitted batch job.

We’ve now submitted and checked a small job. For the analysis job, we’ll use clearer log filenames and optional email notifications.

title: Output files and email notifications
body:
In analysis.sbatch, before executable commands
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=YOUR_NETID@illinois.edu
Illustration: analysis job 123457. Slurm fills in %j.
Program outputOrdinary messages
→
analysis-123457.out
Program diagnosticsErrors and other messages
→
analysis-123457.err
Slurm eventsEND or FAIL
→
Email toYOUR_NETID@illinois.edu
An .err file can also contain progress messages. Read its contents.

%j becomes the job ID. Use your email address, or remove both mail lines.
notes:
These lines let us choose where the job’s messages go. They’re already in the supplied analysis.sbatch template, before the commands that load software and run the analysis.

--output names the file for ordinary program output. --error names the file for error and diagnostic messages. Some programs also put normal progress messages there, so we need to read what the .err file says before calling it a failure.

The useful part of these filenames is %j. Slurm fills that in with the job ID. For job 123457, analysis-%j.out becomes analysis-123457.out. We leave %j in the script; Slurm does the replacement. With these filenames, the logs go into the folder we submit from. If we add a subfolder to the path, that folder needs to exist before submission.

For email, --mail-type selects the events: END for the job ending and FAIL for failure. --mail-user is the recipient, so we put our own address there or remove both mail lines. Delivery depends on the cluster’s email setup. Even with a completion email, we still check the result.

The next two slides cover optional requests, starting with GPUs.

title: When the analysis needs a GPU
body:
Optional GPU job: use your group’s GPU partition and GPU type
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_GPU_PARTITION
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:GPU_TYPE:1
Inside an allocated NVIDIA GPU job
nvidia-smi
--gresRequest GPUs with gpu:TYPE:COUNT; count is per node.
GPU_TYPE / final 1The configured GPU type / one GPU per allocated node.

The tiny demo needs no GPU. Add this only for software that supports and uses one.
notes:
Some analysis tools can use a GPU, which is an additional processor for software that supports GPU computing. If a tool needs one, we first need an account and GPU partition that our group can use.

In --gres=gpu:GPU_TYPE:1, gpu names the resource, GPU_TYPE is the type name configured on the cluster, and the final 1 requests one GPU per allocated node. We get the valid names from the group’s documentation or support contact.

Reserving a GPU won’t make a CPU-only program use it. Inside an allocated NVIDIA GPU job, nvidia-smi shows the GPU visible to that job and some basic usage information. The GPU also has its own memory, separate from the CPU RAM we request with --mem.

The software needs a compatible environment too, so its installation instructions matter here. Our tiny demo stays on CPUs. Another optional setting is asking for a particular compute node; we’ll look at that next, because a node name and a GPU type refer to different things.

title: When a particular node is required
body:
Optional: use a compute-node name your account can access
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --nodelist=NODE_NAME
sinfo: inspect resources; -p selects the partition; -N lists nodes
sinfo -p YOUR_PARTITION -N
--nodes=1How many nodes you request
--nodelistWhich named node you request

Normally let Slurm choose. Name a compute node only when your group requires that machine.
notes:
There are two similar-looking options here, but they mean different things. --nodes=1 says, “I need one computer.” --nodelist=NODE_NAME says, “I need this particular computer.” If we use it, NODE_NAME has to be a real compute node in a partition our account can access. We wouldn't put a login node here.

To look at the available resources, we can use sinfo. The -p option picks a partition, and -N lists the information by node. A node appearing in that list doesn't automatically mean our account has access to it.

For most jobs, I'd let Slurm choose a suitable node. Asking for one specific machine gives the scheduler fewer choices, so we may wait longer. It can make sense if the group needs that machine for a hardware test or comparison. But if we just need more memory or a certain GPU type, we can usually ask for that resource directly.

That's how we choose resources. Next, we'll use them to open a compute shell and prepare our software.

title: Open an interactive compute shell with srun
body:
From the login shell in demo: paste this whole block as one command
srun --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT --partition=YOUR_PARTITION \
  --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 \
  --mem=4G --time=00:15:00 --pty bash
srunStart a program on allocated compute resources.
--pty bashOpen an interactive terminal running the Bash shell.
After the prompt returnshostname should show a compute node; pwd should show the project folder.

A trailing \ continues a command onto the next line; nothing follows it on that line.
notes:
We've been using the login node to organize files and submit jobs. For the software setup, we'll open a shell on a compute node so we can work there directly.

We start from the login shell, in demo. This srun command asks for one node, one task, two CPUs, four GiB of memory, and fifteen minutes. These are example settings for a small setup task. You'd replace YOUR_ACCOUNT and YOUR_PARTITION with the values approved for your group.

Although the command takes up several lines on the slide, it's one command. Each backslash continues onto the next line, and nothing should come after it on that line. srun requests the resources and starts a program. Here, --pty bash gives us an interactive terminal running Bash on those resources.

We may have to wait in the queue. When the prompt appears, hostname should show a compute node, and pwd should still show our project folder. We'll prepare Python in this shell. VS Code's Run button and notebook cells don't automatically move to that compute node just because we've opened this shell.

title: Make Python available in the compute shell
body:
Inside the allocation, in demo; use a version shown as available
module avail python
module load python/3.11.11
module list
CommandMeaning
module avail pythonList cluster modules matching Python
module load python/3.11.11Select this installed Python version for this shell
module listConfirm which cluster modules are loaded

analysis.py needs pandas. Next, create .venv in demo and install pandas there.
notes:
We're now in the compute shell, inside demo. Before we install any packages, we need to choose which Python we're using.

The cluster already has software installed. The module command lets our shell select from those installations. module avail python shows the Python choices. module load python/3.11.11 selects this example version, and module list lets us check what's loaded. The number after the slash is the version. Use one that's actually available, and keep the same version when we write the batch job later.

Having Python available is only part of the setup. Our script, analysis.py, uses pandas to read a table. pandas is a package: reusable code that the script can import. We still need to install it for the Python we're using.

We'll do that inside a project environment. One naming detail before we move on: the cluster's module command and Python's -m option are different things. We'll use -m in the next step.

title: Create a Python environment and install pandas
body:
Continue in the same compute shell and remote demo folder
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install pandas
ls -a
Create .venv-m runs Python’s venv utility; .venv is the new folder.
Activatesource makes this shell use .venv/bin/python.
Install pandas-m pip runs the package installer for the selected Python.

ls -a shows the hidden .venv folder. After pip finishes, check the import on the next slide.
notes:
We’re still in the same compute shell and remote demo folder, with our Python module loaded. python -m venv .venv runs Python’s venv tool and creates the project environment. The -m means run this Python module as a program; it’s different from the cluster’s module command.

source .venv/bin/activate makes this shell use .venv/bin/python. Then python -m pip install pandas runs the installer through that selected Python. Wait for it to finish and for the prompt to return.

ls -a shows hidden names, so we can see .venv too. We create this environment on the cluster; we don’t copy a laptop environment over. Activation selects it for this shell, but doesn’t activate every other shell or job.

Once installation finishes, let’s check that this Python can actually load pandas.

title: Check that pandas imports and save package versions
body:
-c executes the quoted Python code immediately
python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
import pandasCheck that this Python can load the package.
Print versionprint(pandas.__version__) displays the installed version; expect a version number.
freeze lists versions; > writes the file, replacing existing contents
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt

Continue when a version prints without an error. Keep this compute shell open.
notes:
We’re in the same compute shell, with .venv still active. The -c option executes the quoted Python code. import pandas loads the package, the semicolon separates the instructions, and print(pandas.__version__) prints its version.

We want a version number with no import error. If it fails, check the loaded Python module, activation, and any installation error before continuing. Finishing a download doesn’t by itself prove the package can be used.

Then pip freeze lists installed package versions. The greater-than sign writes that list into requirements.txt, replacing the file if it already exists. This records the installation; it doesn’t install anything again.

Keep this compute shell open for a moment. The next diagram shows which files remain after it closes, and why a new shell or job needs activation again.

title: The environment stays; activation is per shell
body:
Install packagespython -m pip install pandasAfter creating and activating .venv
Write files→
Shared project storage
demo/.venv/Python + installed packagesThese files remain.
Activate in each new shell or jobsource .venv/bin/activate
Current compute shell
python→.venv/bin/python
Same existing.venvNo reinstall
A later batch job
python→.venv/bin/python

After setup, exit returns to the login shell; .venv stays in project storage.
notes:
This is a distinction that's easy to mix up: installing a package and activating an environment are two separate steps.

In the top row, pip puts pandas and the packages it depends on into .venv. Those are files in our project storage. They're still there after the compute shell closes.

In the bottom row, activation tells the current shell to use .venv/bin/python. We're selecting files that already exist. We're not reinstalling them, and we're not requesting a compute node. When a batch job starts later, it'll load the same compatible Python module and activate this same environment. Activating it here doesn't activate it in every other terminal or job.

Then, inside a Python program, import pandas loads the installed package so the program can use it.

Our setup is finished, so exit takes us out of the compute shell and releases this interactive allocation. We can check hostname and pwd to confirm we're back on the login node in the project folder. If the allocation has already ended, check the host before typing exit again.

Our .venv is ready for its batch job. Before that, I'll show the alternative you may see in other projects: Conda.

title: Create a Conda environment from a supplied file
body:
Alternative to .venv; \ continues the command on the next line
module avail miniconda3
module load YOUR_CONDA_MODULE
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda run -n analysis \
  python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
environment.ymlRecords the environment name and requested packages
-f environment.ymlRead the environment specification from this file.
-n analysisUse the environment named analysis (from name: analysis in the file).

Choose this instead of .venv. In a new compute shell, expect a pandas version with no error.
notes:
You may download a project and find an environment.yml file with it. That file gives Conda the environment name and the packages to install. You'd use this route instead of creating .venv. We don't need to do both for our example.

Our supplied file is in examples, so it needs to be copied into the remote project first. We'd open a new compute shell for this setup. Conda may use space in home, so run quota to check your usage before starting. If home is nearly full, ask your group's technical contact where the environment should go.

module avail miniconda3 shows the available Conda modules. Replace YOUR_CONDA_MODULE with the one you're going to load. Then conda env create builds the environment, and -f tells it which file to read. Our file names the environment analysis.

In the last command, conda run -n analysis means “run this command in the environment named analysis.” The Python part checks that pandas imports and prints its version. We want that to finish without an error before moving on.

After the check, exit leaves the setup shell. For the next slide, we're returning to the .venv we already prepared and putting its setup into a batch job.

title: Prepare a Python batch job with its environment
body:
1 · Beginning of analysis.sbatch
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis
#SBATCH --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_PARTITION
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=1G
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
2 · Continue in the same file, after the left column
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err

set -e
module load python/3.11.11
source .venv/bin/activate
python analysis.py

set -e stops on setup failure. Set your account and partition, then save analysis.sbatch.
notes:
Our software is ready, so we can put it into a batch job. These two columns are one complete analysis.sbatch file: read down the left, then down the right. All #SBATCH settings go before the executable commands.

Set your approved account and partition, and use the same available Python version as during setup. This small example asks for one node, one task, one CPU, one GiB of memory, and five minutes. Slurm fills %j with the new job ID in the output and error filenames. The supplied template also has email settings; use your own address or remove both email lines.

set -e stops the script if a setup command fails. The job loads Python, activates our existing .venv, and runs analysis.py. It reuses the packages we installed; it doesn’t need to install them again.

Save analysis.sbatch in VS Code. Then we’ll switch to the login terminal and submit that saved file.

title: Submit the analysis job
body:
In the login shell, from the demo folder
pwd
ls data/samples.csv analysis.py analysis.sbatch
sbatch analysis.sbatch
Illustrative analysis job ID; hello used 123456
Submitted batch job 123457
Check whether this new job is pending or running
squeue -u YOUR_NETID

Use the returned ID in analysis-JOBID.out and analysis-JOBID.err.
notes:
We’re back in the login shell in demo, and analysis.sbatch is saved. pwd checks our location. The ls command checks that the input, Python script, and batch file are there. Then sbatch analysis.sbatch submits the saved request.

The example response is Submitted batch job 123457. Keep the number you actually receive: this is a new job, separate from hello.

squeue -u YOUR_NETID checks your jobs, just as before. Use the new ID in analysis-JOBID.out and analysis-JOBID.err. Those logs may not appear until the job starts.

Once a log exists, we can follow its output on the next page.

title: Follow job output with tail
body:
After the job starts and its log exists; use your actual job ID
tail -n 20 analysis-123457.out
tail -f analysis-123457.out

-n 20: show the last 20 lines · -f: keep following new output

Batch job 123457 Keeps running
writes→
Log fileanalysis-123457.out
read by→
Terminal log viewer tail -f
Ctrl+CStops viewing
The job and log viewer are separate processes.

To cancel the analysis job itself: scancel 123457.
notes:
Once the log exists, tail lets us check its latest output. Use the current job’s ID in the filename. tail -n 20 shows the last twenty lines and gives us the prompt back. tail -f stays open and shows new lines as the program writes them.

The diagram shows why watching a job and running a job are separate. The batch job writes the file; tail reads that file from our terminal. While tail -f is running, this terminal is busy watching it. Ctrl+C stops that viewer so we can type another command. It doesn’t cancel the submitted job.

If we actually want to stop the batch job, we use scancel followed by its ID. We’ll let the analysis continue here. After leaving the viewer, let’s check its error log.

title: Search the error log with grep
body:
After Ctrl+C stops the tail viewer; use your actual job ID
grep -in "error" analysis-123457.err
-iIgnore letter case: error also matches Error.
-nShow the matching line number.
Illustrative error: the matching message is on line 8
8:FileNotFoundError: data/samples.csv

Read the surrounding log. No match does not prove success; .err can also contain progress messages.
notes:
We’re back at the shell prompt. grep searches inside the error log. Here, -in combines two options: -i ignores letter case, and -n shows the line number. We’re looking for text containing error.

The example output is an illustration of a failed run, not the expected output of our successful demo. The 8 before the colon means line eight. FileNotFoundError points us toward the path data/samples.csv. We’d open the log and read the surrounding lines before changing anything.

A search is only a way to find relevant text. No match doesn’t prove success, and a nonempty .err file doesn’t always mean failure; some programs put normal progress messages there.

Once the job finishes, we also need to check the actual result. Let’s open that in VS Code next.

title: Open the result in VS Code
body:
Illustration · expected result from the supplied demo
EXPLORER · DEMO
▸ data
1 ▾ results2 summary.csvanalysis.py
analysis.sbatch
summary.csv
1samples,total_reads23,3700
3

3 input samples
3,700 total reads

Read it here. No download needed.
For a local copy: right-click the remote file → Download…

Other viewers: logs and images open directly;
Rainbow CSV colors columns; PDF/Jupyter extensions open those files.
notes:
We can go straight back to Explorer to look at the result. It's the same VS Code window we've been using. Refresh the folder if needed, expand results, and open the output table.

This illustration shows the result we expect from the supplied demo. First expand results, then click summary.csv. The header is samples,total_reads, and the single summary row is 3,3700. That means three input samples and 3,700 reads in total. We are checking the sample count in the first column, not counting three rows in the output. If the file is empty or looks incomplete, we'd go back to the logs to find out why.

We can read the file right here on the cluster. If we want a copy on the laptop, we can right-click summary.csv and choose Download.

The viewer depends on the file type. Text and images open directly. Rainbow CSV adds colors that help separate table columns. PDFs and notebooks use suitable extensions. When installing one, follow the prompt for the local or SSH environment.

Opening a notebook is just opening the file. It doesn't reserve compute resources. Check where its cells will run, and keep substantial analysis off the login node.

We've followed a Python job through to its result. The same basic process works for R too.

title: Run an R script as a Slurm batch job
body:
R commands below the #SBATCH resource settings
module load R
Rscript analysis.R
Copy analysis.R and analysis_R.sbatch into the project; set the account and partition
sbatch analysis_R.sbatch
Same inputdata/samples.csv
R outputresults/summary_R.csv

This example uses base R; no additional package installation is needed.
notes:
If you mainly work in R, the Slurm part will look very familiar. We still submit a batch file, check the queue, and read the logs. We change the software we load and the command that runs our script.

The examples folder includes analysis.R and analysis_R.sbatch. Copy them into the remote project that contains data/samples.csv, and put your approved account and partition into the batch file.

Inside that file, module load R selects the cluster's R installation. Use an R module name that's available on the system. Rscript analysis.R runs the saved script, so we don't need to open an interactive R console.

This particular example uses only base R, which means it doesn't need extra packages or a custom package library. If your own script uses additional packages, those need to be prepared before the job runs. Our example writes its result to results/summary_R.csv.

After sbatch returns a job ID, the routine is the same: check the queue and logs, then open the result. If something goes wrong along the way, the error message usually tells us where to start looking.

title: Common errors and the first useful check
body:
What you seeCheck first
No such file or directoryRun pwd; check the path and filename capitalization.
Command not foundCheck spelling; load the module or activate the environment.
No module named… / no package called…Select the intended Python/R environment; install the missing package there.
OUT_OF_MEMORY / TIMEOUTCompare --mem / --time with the tool’s documented requirements.
Invalid account / partitionUse your approved --account and matching --partition.
Permission denied / quota exceededRun quota; confirm the group gave you write access to that folder.
notes:
Errors are part of getting a job set up. The useful thing is to look at the message before submitting the same file again, because an unchanged submission will usually hit the same problem.

If a file can't be found, I'd check pwd, then the path and the spelling, including capital letters. If a command can't be found, check its spelling and whether the right module or environment is selected. For a missing Python or R package, check the environment the job actually uses, and install the package there.

OUT_OF_MEMORY means the job exceeded its memory allowance. TIMEOUT means it reached its time limit. Look at --mem or --time alongside the error log and the software's documented requirements before changing the request.

For an invalid account or partition, check that they're an approved pair. For a quota error, quota shows usage and limits. For Permission denied, ask your group to confirm that you can write to that folder.

And when you ask for help, include the job ID, the batch script, the exact error, and the software version. Those details give your lab contact or ICC support something useful to work with. They don't need your password or a copy of the whole dataset.

For account-specific problems, ICC support can check things a general tutorial can't. Send the job ID and exact error, along with the relevant job file and software version.

We've gone from connecting to the cluster all the way to opening a result: choose a project folder, prepare the software, request resources, submit the script, then check the logs and output. Our examples are deliberately small. For your own analysis, replace the placeholders and choose software versions and resources that fit the project.

That gives you a starting point for running your own work on the Campus Cluster. Thanks, everyone.
